title: React Best Practices
description: React and Next.js guidance for waterfalls, bundles, rendering, and data fetching.
author: Vercel
why: A focused performance reference with individual rules and concrete code examples.
note: Use only with the matching React/Next.js versions. Linked upstream, not copied; this snapshot has an MIT declaration but no standalone repository license file.
outcome: React and Next.js guidance for waterfalls, bundles, rendering, and data fetching.

title: React Composition Patterns
description: Design flexible component APIs with compound components, lifted state, and composition.
author: Vercel
why: Targets the component-design decisions that become painful as a UI library grows.
note: The React 19 section does not apply to React 18. Linked upstream; use the full package with its rules.
outcome: Design flexible component APIs with compound components, lifted state, and composition.

title: Frontend Design
description: Develop an intentional visual direction, typography, and layout for a specific product.
author: Anthropic
why: Complements code-quality skills with a deliberate design process rather than a generic UI template.
note: Upstream design guidance is opinionated. The actual brief and existing design system still control the work.
outcome: Develop an intentional visual direction, typography, and layout for a specific product.

title: Web Interface Review
description: Review interface code against accessibility, interaction, navigation, and usability guidelines.
author: Vercel
why: Adds a review pass for the details a successful build cannot catch.
note: Fetches a separate live guideline document. Pinning this skill does not pin that remote document; this is not an accessibility certification.
outcome: Review interface code against accessibility, interaction, navigation, and usability guidelines.

title: Search Before You Build
description: Compare existing packages, patterns, and tools before writing a custom implementation.
author: Affaan Mustafa and ECC contributors
why: Makes adopt, extend, and build an explicit decision instead of defaulting to more code.
note: Search channels and researcher-agent names depend on the host. Upstream package examples still need verification.
outcome: Compare existing packages, patterns, and tools before writing a custom implementation.

title: Systematic Debugging
description: Investigate root causes, test hypotheses, and verify a fix before changing more code.
author: Jesse Vincent and Superpowers contributors
why: A disciplined alternative to speculative patches, with supporting debugging techniques in the package.
note: References other Superpowers skills that are not all bundled here. Helper scripts are copied as source and have not been executed.
outcome: Investigate root causes, test hypotheses, and verify a fix before changing more code.

title: Test-Driven Development
description: Turn planned behavior into RED/GREEN test evidence and a reviewable implementation.
author: Affaan Mustafa and ECC contributors
why: Connects the plan, the tests, and the implementation instead of treating test coverage as an afterthought.
note: Coverage targets and example commands are upstream conventions, not this collection’s guarantees. Use project-owned validation and approval rules.
outcome: Turn planned behavior into RED/GREEN test evidence and a reviewable implementation.

title: Web App Testing
description: Exercise local web applications with Playwright, screenshots, console logs, and server helpers.
author: Anthropic
why: Provides concrete browser-testing examples rather than stopping at a compiler or build check.
note: Includes Python helper scripts and examples. Review them before execution; do not treat upstream black-box advice as a reason to skip source review.
outcome: Exercise local web applications with Playwright, screenshots, console logs, and server helpers.

title: Verification Loop
description: Review build, types, lint, tests, security checks, and the final diff before handoff.
author: Affaan Mustafa and ECC contributors
why: A broad completion checklist that is useful after a cross-cutting change.
note: Full verification can be expensive. Adapt it to actual project commands; not every check applies to every edit.
outcome: Review build, types, lint, tests, security checks, and the final diff before handoff.

title: Evidence Before Completion
description: Require fresh command output before claiming a change is fixed, passing, or complete.
author: Jesse Vincent and Superpowers contributors
why: Addresses unsupported completion claims independently of the particular test framework.
note: Instructions do not enforce a security or CI boundary. Keep claims scoped to the checks actually executed.
outcome: Require fresh command output before claiming a change is fixed, passing, or complete.

title: Working in Git Worktrees
description: Detect existing workspace isolation and establish an owned worktree when needed.
author: Jesse Vincent and Superpowers contributors
why: Useful for avoiding branch collisions when engineering tasks run concurrently.
note: A worktree is not an OS sandbox. Setup commands must respect the repository’s package manager and permissions.
outcome: Detect existing workspace isolation and establish an owned worktree when needed.

title: API Design
description: Review REST resources, HTTP semantics, pagination, errors, versioning, and rate limits.
author: Affaan Mustafa and ECC contributors
why: A practical checklist for consistent public APIs and integration boundaries.
note: These are design conventions and examples, not a substitute for an executable API contract.
requires: API requirements or an existing contract
outcome: Review REST resources, HTTP semantics, pagination, errors, versioning, and rate limits.

title: Go Development Patterns
description: Use idiomatic Go error handling, interfaces, concurrency, and package structure.
author: Affaan Mustafa and ECC contributors
why: A language-specific companion to general agent instructions for backend engineering.
note: Review examples against the consuming project’s Go version and constraints.
requires: Go source or a Go project
outcome: Use idiomatic Go error handling, interfaces, concurrency, and package structure.

title: Go Testing Patterns
description: Write table-driven tests, subtests, benchmarks, fuzz tests, and coverage checks in Go.
author: Affaan Mustafa and ECC contributors
why: Adds concrete language-specific testing patterns beyond a generic TDD prompt.
note: Example tool versions and coverage thresholds are not automatically appropriate for a new project.
outcome: Write table-driven tests, subtests, benchmarks, fuzz tests, and coverage checks in Go.

title: Postgres Best Practices
description: Review SQL, indexing, connection management, schema design, locking, and row-level security.
author: Supabase
why: Brings database-specific guidance and detailed reference files into the same collection as application skills.
note: Some guidance is Supabase-specific. Example performance figures are not benchmarks from Jordan’s environment.
outcome: Review SQL, indexing, connection management, schema design, locking, and row-level security.

title: Document Co-Authoring
description: Structure technical documents through context gathering, refinement, and reader testing.
author: Anthropic
why: A useful companion for the articles and technical specifications that explain engineering work.
note: Linked only: no package-level license file was present in this snapshot. Do not infer redistribution terms from neighboring skills.
outcome: Structure technical documents through context gathering, refinement, and reader testing.

title: Skills CLI
description: Discover and selectively install skill packages with an existing open-source command-line tool.
author: Vercel
note: Review the installer and selected package revision. Listing is different from installing; avoid blanket global installs.
outcome: Read the upstream documentation and evaluate the specific component you need.
why: Reuse an existing selective installer instead of creating another package manager.

outcome: Read the upstream documentation and evaluate the specific component you need.
why: Keep workspace discovery and affected-task analysis close to the actual project graph.
